table.header: Most unpredictability indices are positively correlated with each other
table.expanded: Self-report and administrative neighborhood threat show opposite associations with working memory capacity CBS-derived administrative neighborhood threat, quantified as the average exposure to crime across districts that individuals have lived in, is positively associated with working memory capacity (β = 0.11, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.05, 0.17], p = .002).

table.header: Most unpredictability indices are positively correlated with each other
table.expanded: In contrast, LISS self-reported neighborhood threat is negatively associated with working memory capacity (β = -0.145, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.05], p = .017).

table.header: Most unpredictability indices are positively correlated with each other
table.expanded: Similarly, a LISS adversity composite consisting of the individual LISS-adversity measures is negatively associated with working memory capacity (β = -0.147, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.25, -0.05], p = .004).

table.header: Most unpredictability indices are positively correlated with each other
table.expanded: Diverging patterns across adversity dimensions: Information processing is positively associated with administrative unpredictability, but negatively with self-reported cumulative adversity and neighborhood threat CBS-derived administrative crime victimization is negatively associated with information processing (β = -0.1, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.16, -0.03], p = .01), suggesting less efficient general information processing, in line with a deficit pattern.

table.header: Most unpredictability indices are positively correlated with each other
table.expanded: CBS-derived unpredictability in monthly crime rates is positively associated with general information processing (β = 0.08, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.15], p = .025).

table.header: Most unpredictability indices are positively correlated with each other
table.expanded: In line with our working memory findings, both LISS self-reported neighborhood threat (β = -0.14, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.21, -0.06], p = .002) and the LISS adversity composite (β = -0.15, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.06], p = .001) are negatively associated with information processing, in line with a deficit pattern.

table.header: Most unpredictability indices are positively correlated with each other

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 623 columns across 56 data files.
#### Issues Identified
2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 56 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### File paths

**5 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `H:\\project\\code\\functions.R` to `functions.R` (in EF_analysis_covSeq.R); `H:\\project\\code\\functions.R` to `functions.R` (in WM_analysis_covSeq.R); `H:\\project\\code\\functions.R` to `functions.R` (in WM_analysis.R); `H:\\project\\code\\functions.R` to `functions.R` (in output_prep_EF.R); `H:\\project\\code\\functions.R` to `functions.R` (in EF_analysis.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 7 references matched several files sharing a name and could not be resolved by study group or folder; they were left unrewritten and flagged. **27 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved 9 of 27 on a best-effort basis; 18 could not be resolved and were left unrewritten (the script runs against the original, un-rewritten call and will likely fail.

**`setwd()` in the code**

**15 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 Python code file.
#### Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no `source()`-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an `import` loads a module, not the paper's own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

text.formatted: Preprint: This paper has been preprinted on PsyArXiv (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/v3a95_v1">https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/v3a95_v1</ref>).

text.text: Adverse experiences can influence the brain and behavior across the lifespan.
For instance, childhood adversity is associated with cognitive outcomes well into adulthood, including lower executive functioning and related cognitive processes [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] .
text.formatted: For instance, childhood adversity is associated with cognitive outcomes well into adulthood, including lower executive functioning and related cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[6]</ref> .

text.text: Moreover, even experiencing adversity in adulthood, such as financial hardship or threat, can affect cognitive processes 7, 8.
text.formatted: Moreover, even experiencing adversity in adulthood, such as financial hardship or threat, can affect cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">8</ref>.

text.text: Most of these studies have measured adversity using self-reports 9, 10 ; for example, adults retrospectively reporting on their childhood experiences.
text.formatted: Most of these studies have measured adversity using self-reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">10</ref> ; for example, adults retrospectively reporting on their childhood experiences.

text.text: Such self-reports are valuable because they capture individuals' perceptions of experiences 11 .
text.formatted: Such self-reports are valuable because they capture individuals' perceptions of experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11</ref> .

text.text: Such perceptions are known to predict various outcomes: for instance, perceptions of social standing predict health outcomes above and beyond more 'objective' measures of socioeconomic status (education, income, and occupation) 12 , and perceived social rank alone can produce divergent health trajectories in identical twins 13 .
text.formatted: Such perceptions are known to predict various outcomes: for instance, perceptions of social standing predict health outcomes above and beyond more 'objective' measures of socioeconomic status (education, income, and occupation) <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12</ref> , and perceived social rank alone can produce divergent health trajectories in identical twins <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">13</ref> .

text.text: Similarly, whether individuals perceive stressors as controllable or predictable is associated with reduced trauma-related symptoms 14.
text.formatted: Similarly, whether individuals perceive stressors as controllable or predictable is associated with reduced trauma-related symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14</ref>.

text.text: Yet, self-reports alone cannot fully characterize individuals' experiences.
Work on adverse childhood experiences has documented systematic underreporting and sizable measurement error in retrospective measures 9 .
text.formatted: Work on adverse childhood experiences has documented systematic underreporting and sizable measurement error in retrospective measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">9</ref> .

text.text: Relatedly, prospective and retrospective indicators of childhood maltreatment frequently disagree within the same individual 15 .
text.formatted: Relatedly, prospective and retrospective indicators of childhood maltreatment frequently disagree within the same individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> .

text.text: One reason for this discrepancy is that retrospective measures can be biased by factors such as current depressive symptoms and current family closeness 16 .
text.formatted: One reason for this discrepancy is that retrospective measures can be biased by factors such as current depressive symptoms and current family closeness <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16</ref> .

text.text: These findings underscore the need for complementary, more objective measures.
Here, we define objective measures as the verifiable external triggers (e.g., experiences, events, or circumstances) that give rise to selfreported outcomes.
For example, a traumatic experience (the objective trigger) may elicit a self-reported elevation in perceived stress.
Empirically, objective triggers could be inferred by continuously tracking individuals and their surrounding environments across time.

In animal ecology, such continuous tracking of individuals and their environments is increasingly realized: GPS and biologging technologies can generate millions of locationand sensor-linked data points per animal, treating the animal and its ecology as a dynamically developing system [17] [18] [19] [20] [21].
text.formatted: In animal ecology, such continuous tracking of individuals and their environments is increasingly realized: GPS and biologging technologies can generate millions of locationand sensor-linked data points per animal, treating the animal and its ecology as a dynamically developing system <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21]</ref>.

text.text: In many countries, an analogue to continuous tracking already exists for humans in the form of administrative records.
These government-managed records can hold information about individuals' residence, occupation, finances, family composition, law enforcement encounters, healthcare spending, and more.
Thanks to digitization and advances in data storage and processing, it has become easier for researchers to tap into these records.

A growing number of studies now link self-reports with administrative records, for example by linking individuals' self-reported experiences of childhood abuse with official records from child protective services.
Such studies consistently report poor agreement between the two data sources and conclude that they identify partially distinct groups who go on to experience worse outcomes 15 .
text.formatted: Such studies consistently report poor agreement between the two data sources and conclude that they identify partially distinct groups who go on to experience worse outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> .

text.text: Relatedly, combining 'objective' administrative records with 'subjective' self-reported experiences of childhood adversity has been shown to better predict later mental-health problems than either source alone 22, 23 .
text.formatted: Relatedly, combining 'objective' administrative records with 'subjective' self-reported experiences of childhood adversity has been shown to better predict later mental-health problems than either source alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">23</ref> .

text.text: Together, these findings highlight that self-report and administrative data capture different, complementary facets of adversity, and that studying them side-by-side may reveal patterns that we would otherwise miss 24.
text.formatted: Together, these findings highlight that self-report and administrative data capture different, complementary facets of adversity, and that studying them side-by-side may reveal patterns that we would otherwise miss <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24</ref>.

text.text: In recent years, developmental research has also increasingly started to incorporate measures of individuals' surrounding ecologies.

Nowadays, many studies include neighborhood-level indicators, such as socioeconomic variables, infrastructure and green space availability scores, or crime statistics of areas in which individuals live, to explain children's outcomes 25, 26 .
text.formatted: Nowadays, many studies include neighborhood-level indicators, such as socioeconomic variables, infrastructure and green space availability scores, or crime statistics of areas in which individuals live, to explain children's outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26</ref> .

text.text: These studies have provided insights into the importance of neighborhood context for children's development.
In particular, a growing literature further links neighborhood characteristics to physical and mental health, brain development, and cognition [27] [28] [29] [30] [31] [32] [33] [34] .
text.formatted: In particular, a growing literature further links neighborhood characteristics to physical and mental health, brain development, and cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[30]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[34]</ref> .

text.text: For example, large-scale work like the Moving to Opportunity study demonstrates that sustained exposure to low-poverty neighborhoods causally improves later earnings and education 35 .
text.formatted: For example, large-scale work like the Moving to Opportunity study demonstrates that sustained exposure to low-poverty neighborhoods causally improves later earnings and education <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">35</ref> .

text.text: Yet, these studies often rely either on aggregates of environmental conditions across large geographical areas or snapshots at one time point.
Consequently, these studies rarely track individuals and their environments as a jointly developing system across time.
Our paper addresses these gaps by linking repeated self-report measures with administrative data both at the individual and neighborhood level.

Specifically, we track individuals and their environments across time, combining self-reports with administrative records to study associations between multiple facets of adversity exposures and cognition.

We are unaware of studies contrasting self-report and administrative measures in the cognitive sciences, though the broader question of whether data source shapes conclusions is well-established in health and developmental psychopathology 15, 22, 36.
text.formatted: We are unaware of studies contrasting self-report and administrative measures in the cognitive sciences, though the broader question of whether data source shapes conclusions is well-established in health and developmental psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">36</ref>.

text.text: Our contribution is to extend this question to the domain of adult cognition, leveraging rich longitudinal data.

To this end, we link approximately 10 years of repeated self-reported adversity measures from the Dutch Longitudinal Internet Studies for the Social Sciences (LISS) panel 37 -a representative longitudinal Dutch internet panel study-with repeated administrative measures of the same constructs derived from Dutch registers governed by Statistics Netherlands (CBS).
text.formatted: To this end, we link approximately 10 years of repeated self-reported adversity measures from the Dutch Longitudinal Internet Studies for the Social Sciences (LISS) panel <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">37</ref> -a representative longitudinal Dutch internet panel study-with repeated administrative measures of the same constructs derived from Dutch registers governed by Statistics Netherlands (CBS).

text.text: Table 1 describes our four adversity dimensions of interest: neighborhood threat, crime victimization, material deprivation, and health as a proxy for morbidity.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> describes our four adversity dimensions of interest: neighborhood threat, crime victimization, material deprivation, and health as a proxy for morbidity.

text.text: From these dimensions, we additionally compute a self-report adversity composite and an administrative adversity composite.
Additionally, we apply a novel framework for quantifying unpredictability in repeated measures data 38 .
text.formatted: Additionally, we apply a novel framework for quantifying unpredictability in repeated measures data <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">38</ref> .

text.text: Unpredictability, often defined as random variation in adversity across time, is increasingly being recognized as a distinct adversity dimension 39, 40 .
text.formatted: Unpredictability, often defined as random variation in adversity across time, is increasingly being recognized as a distinct adversity dimension <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">40</ref> .

text.text: We compute unpredictability in crime rates across individuals' residential histories as our fifth administrative adversity dimension.
Unfortunately, we do not have access to a self-report counterpart.

Our approach aligns with two trends: a growing interest in unpredictability and a shift towards complementing self-report measures (e.g. from the Questionnaire of Unpredictability in Childhood 41 ) with statistical measures capturing random variation in adversity across time 38, [42] [43] [44] .
text.formatted: Our approach aligns with two trends: a growing interest in unpredictability and a shift towards complementing self-report measures (e.g. from the Questionnaire of Unpredictability in Childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">41</ref> ) with statistical measures capturing random variation in adversity across time <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">38,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[42]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[43]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[44]</ref> .

text.text: This emerging research uses different operationalizations of unpredictability that may tap into distinct aspects of unpredictability.

Some measures capture the extent to which individuals can anticipate gradual changes in adversity (e.g. autocorrelation), whereas others capture irregularities, including sudden peaks and valleys (e.g. entropy, changepoints).

These different types of unpredictable changes may pose distinct adaptive challenges: gradual changes may allow individuals to recalibrate expectations incrementally, whereas abrupt shifts demand rapid reorganization of behavioral strategies 39 .
text.formatted: These different types of unpredictable changes may pose distinct adaptive challenges: gradual changes may allow individuals to recalibrate expectations incrementally, whereas abrupt shifts demand rapid reorganization of behavioral strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">39</ref> .

text.text: As the field develops and more studies operationalize unpredictability in different ways, we will gain a clearer picture of how each type shapes developmental outcomes.
Our study examines associations between self-reported adversity with executive functioning processes and working memory abilities, leveraging two existing datasets 8, 45 .
text.formatted: Our study examines associations between self-reported adversity with executive functioning processes and working memory abilities, leveraging two existing datasets <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">45</ref> .

text.text: The executive functioning dataset 8 used cognitive modelling (specifically DDM 46 ) to compute the efficiency (speed and accuracy) of information processing 47, 48 (drift rate), response caution and, nondecision time across several cognitive tasks (measuring inhibition and attention-shifting).

text.text: Further, in line with previous work 8, 45 , we explore three potential patterns of 199 associations between adversity and cognitive outcomes: enhancements (higher adversity is 200 associated with better cognitive performance), impairments (higher adversity is associated 201 with worse cognitive performance), and practical equivalence (cognitive performance is the 202 same across adversity exposures; although it can be realized through different cognitive 203 processes [53] [54] [55] ).

text.text: This three-pronged approach reflects a broader paradigm shift towards more 204 balance in developmental research on adversity 56, 57 .

text.text: This paradigm proposes that adversity 205 does not only impair cognitive functioning, but also tailors specific cognitive abilities to particular types of adversity.
Some studies have documented enhanced attention shifting by youth living in unpredictable environments, potentially an adaptive response to that particular environmental demand [58] [59] [60] .

This study links two data sources: data from the LISS panel (Dutch Longitudinal Internet studies for the Social Sciences) and CBS (Statistics Netherlands).

Our self-report adversity and cognitive outcome measures were obtained from the LISS panel, a representative probability sample of approximately 5,000 Dutch households (around 7,500 individuals) drawn from the population register by Statistics Netherlands (CBS).
Participants annually complete a standardized core battery of questionnaires covering topics such as financial situation and health over the preceding year.
Additionally, participants may opt into a varying selection of monthly studies.
Here, we use data from two samples of semirandomly sampled participants from the LISS panel used in two previous studies 8, 45 .
text.formatted: Here, we use data from two samples of semirandomly sampled participants from the LISS panel used in two previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">45</ref> .

text.text: To ensure socioeconomic diversity within the sample, 50% of participants were sampled from lower socioeconomic strata, indexed by monthly income and educational attainment.
Additionally, the samples only included participants if they had given permission to link their LISS data to CBS microdata.
In both studies, the researchers collected new data (additional adversity measures and cognitive measures) from the samples.

We will refer to the samples as the WM (working memory 45 , N= 737, median age at the time of measurement = 43) and EF (executive functioning 8 , N = 1024, median age at the time of measurement = 40.5) sample.

This is because after encrypting the data (done by CBS), not all individuals from the LISS panel could be identified in CBS.

Our administrative adversity measures were computed based on data from CBS who manages data from Dutch registers on population, income, health, welfare, education, employment, housing, taxes, insurance, and more.
In this study we link individuals from both LISS samples to a subset of microdatasets relating to residential history, individual crime experiences, income, employment, and health (see below).
By definition, microdata refer to data that can be linked to individuals, businesses, and addresses.

Additionally, we use publicly available CBS data (i.e. data that is not linked to individuals), to link monthly crime data to individuals' residential histories (only available through microdata) in CBS.
This allows us to construct time-series of crime rate exposures.

As monthly crime data were only started to be published in 2012 (https://politieopendata.cbs.nl/portal.html?_la=nl&_catalog=Politie&graphtype=Table&tableId=47022NED&_theme=115), we restricted all of our data sources from LISS and CBS to the range between 2012/2013 and 2022 (for the WM sample as the cognitive outcome was collected in 2023) and 2023 (for the EF sample as the cognitive outcome was collected in 2024). raw data, but researchers affiliated with a recognized research institute can apply for access 276 https://liss.statements.centerdata.nl/ (see supplements, Table S0 for links to all used datasets).

We use P-values to test for significance of bivariate correlations (α = 0.05).
We test for three types of associations between different adversity dimensions with working memory and executive functioning outcomes: enhancements, impairments, or practical equivalence.
Enhancements correspond to a positive association between adversity and cognitive outcomes.
Impairments correspond to a negative association between adversity and cognitive outcomes.
Practical equivalence corresponds to a standardized regression coefficients that significantly falls between -0.10 and 0.10, tested using the two one-sided ttests procedure 64 .
text.formatted: Practical equivalence corresponds to a standardized regression coefficients that significantly falls between -0.10 and 0.10, tested using the two one-sided ttests procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">64</ref> .

text.text: This test indicates whether the coefficient is significantly larger than the lower bound and significantly smaller than the upper bound.
The ±0.10 bound was adopted from the power analyses conducted in the two prior studies using these samples 8, 45 , which were powered to detect effects of β = 0.10 with ≥90% power.
text.formatted: The ±0.10 bound was adopted from the power analyses conducted in the two prior studies using these samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">45</ref> , which were powered to detect effects of β = 0.10 with ≥90% power.

text.text: This bound therefore represents the smallest effect size these studies were designed to detect reliably, providing a samplespecific justification rather than an arbitrary default.

We acknowledge that a more principled smallest-effect-size-of-interest argument grounded in the cognitive science literature would further strengthen this choice, and we encourage future work to develop such benchmarks for adversity-cognition research.

In case that both the self-report and administrative adversity measure emerge as significant predictors in any given model, we conclude that the predictor with the higher absolute standardized effect size matters more.

Both for the WM and the EF models, we use the Benjamin-Hochberg procedure to adjust Pvalues for false discovery rate across adversity dimensions within the same research question (RQ2, RQ3, RQ5) and data source (LISS vs CBS).
This approach ensures that we correct for false discovery rate for each of our hypotheses 65 .
text.formatted: This approach ensures that we correct for false discovery rate for each of our hypotheses <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">65</ref> .

text.text: Effectively, this means that we adjust P-values across all of the adversity measures listed in RQ2 separately for LISS and CBS measures.

As we have separate research questions for our unpredictability composite (RQ3) and our cumulative adversity composites (RQ5) and each data source only supplies one measure per data source, we do not need to apply a correction in this case.

text.text: Given the scope of the study and the large amount of measures we could hypothetically derive from the CBS data, we decided to not conduct large-scale sensitivity analyses.

However, in light of some of our findings we decided to deviate from our preregistration and conduct sensitivity analyses to examine the association between CBS-derived neighborhood threat and unpredictability with cognitive outcomes.
Specifically, we reran analyses examining associations between these variables with three different ways of preprocessing the crime data outlined in Table 3.

text.text: Additionally, we reran the analyses controlling for the number of repeated crime measures used per individual and a variable indicating the average urbanization level across neighborhoods individuals lived in.

Lastly, we reran the analyses involving the unpredictability composite with a composite without entropy, which was the only unpredictability index which was negatively associated with all other indices.
We describe the results of these analyses in the supplements (Tables S10-S13).

text.text: In both samples, there are low to moderate positive correlations among LISS-and CBSderived adversity measures of the same adversity construct (Figure 1).
text.formatted: In both samples, there are low to moderate positive correlations among LISS-and CBSderived adversity measures of the same adversity construct (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">1</ref>).

text.text: Significant correlations between adversity constructs tend to cluster within the LISS and CBS measures respectively, with fewer correlations emerging across data sources.
Across all possible bivariate associations, correlations involving LISS self-report measures tend to be higher.
We note, that these correlations have not been corrected for multiple testing.
In both samples, there are low to moderate positive correlations among unpredictability indices derived from monthly CBS crime rates (Figure 2).
text.formatted: In both samples, there are low to moderate positive correlations among unpredictability indices derived from monthly CBS crime rates (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">2</ref>).

text.text: Notably, only entropy, measuring the complexity of a time series (Table 2), is consistently negatively associated with all other unpredictability indices.
text.formatted: Notably, only entropy, measuring the complexity of a time series (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>), is consistently negatively associated with all other unpredictability indices.

text.text: Thus, in both samples, time series showing more variability (higher coefficient of variation, more changepoints in mean and variance) and lower predictability after removing systematic trends (lower absolute autocorrelation and color of noise), tended to contain redundancies (e.g. self-similar sequences), making them less complex.

Self-report and administrative neighborhood threat show opposite associations with working memory capacity CBS-derived administrative neighborhood threat, quantified as the average exposure to crime across districts that individuals have lived in, is positively associated with working memory capacity (β = 0.11, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.05, 0.17], p = .002).
Thus, adults who lived in neighborhoods with higher monthly crime rates showed better working memory capacity, implying enhanced performance.
This effect was qualitatively similar across the three different ways in which we preprocessed the monthly crime rates (see methods; results in supplements Table S10).
text.formatted: This effect was qualitatively similar across the three different ways in which we preprocessed the monthly crime rates (see methods; results in supplements Table <ref type="table">S10</ref>).

text.text: Moreover, the effect holds after controlling for the number of repeated crime measures used per individual and the average urbanity level across districts (supplements Table S10).
text.formatted: Moreover, the effect holds after controlling for the number of repeated crime measures used per individual and the average urbanity level across districts (supplements Table <ref type="table">S10</ref>).

text.text: In contrast, LISS self-reported neighborhood threat is negatively associated with working memory capacity (β = -0.145, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.05], p = .017).

Similarly, a LISS adversity composite consisting of the individual LISS-adversity measures is negatively associated with working memory capacity (β = -0.147, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.25, -0.05], p = .004).
Together this suggests that adults who self-report higher neighborhood threat exposure or more adversity overall, show worse working memory capacity.
These findings are in line with a deficit pattern.
We find no other associations among adversity measures and working memory components (Figure 3, supplements Table S6 for complete results).
text.formatted: We find no other associations among adversity measures and working memory components (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">3</ref>, supplements Table <ref type="table">S6</ref> for complete results).

text.text: Diverging patterns across adversity dimensions: Information processing is positively associated with administrative unpredictability, but negatively with self-reported cumulative adversity and neighborhood threat CBS-derived administrative crime victimization is negatively associated with information processing (β = -0.1, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.16, -0.03], p = .01), suggesting less efficient general information processing, in line with a deficit pattern.
CBS-derived unpredictability in monthly crime rates is positively associated with general information processing (β = 0.08, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.15] , p = .025).
This effect was qualitatively similar across two out of three different ways in which we preprocessed the monthly crime rates (see methods).
The method which resulted in imputing a large amount of zeros for some of the participants, resulted in a significant effect in the opposite direction (supplements Table S12).
text.formatted: The method which resulted in imputing a large amount of zeros for some of the participants, resulted in a significant effect in the opposite direction (supplements Table <ref type="table">S12</ref>).

text.text: This preprocessing method makes some of the time series in the sample more stable, which may explain the flipped sign of the association.

The original positive effect holds after controlling for the number of repeated measures used per individual, the average urbanity level across districts, and after removing entropy from the composite (supplements Table S12).
text.formatted: The original positive effect holds after controlling for the number of repeated measures used per individual, the average urbanity level across districts, and after removing entropy from the composite (supplements Table <ref type="table">S12</ref>).

text.text: Thus, our results suggest that individuals who experience more unpredictability in neighborhood crime rates show more efficient general information processing, implying enhanced performance.

In line with our working memory findings, both LISS self-reported neighborhood threat (β = -0.14, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.21, -0.06], p = .002) and the LISS adversity composite (β = -0.15, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.06], p = .001) are negatively associated with information processing, in line with a deficit pattern.
We find no other associations among adversity measures and executive functioning parameters (Figure 4, supplements Table S8 for complete results).

text.text: These associations reflect the covariation between covariates and cognitive outcomes after accounting for adversity exposures, and should not be interpreted as direct or causal effects given the observational nature of our data.

There are negative associations among age and environmental noise during the experiment with working memory capacity: older individuals and individuals who experience a noisy environment during cognitive testing tend to show worse working memory capacity.
There is a positive association between income-to-needs ratio and working memory updating, such that individuals from higher socioeconomic strata tend to show better working memory updating.

Similarly, there are positive associations between education and working memory capacity and executive functioning information processing: individuals who completed higher education, tend to show better working memory capacity and more efficient general information processing.
Unexpectedly, there are consistent negative associations among education and working memory updating: individuals with lower education tend to show better working memory updating.
Notably, all these associations are partly mediated through our adversity exposure variables.
This means that adversity may account for some, but not all, of the observed covariation between sociodemographic characteristics and cognitive performance.
With the exception of sex in the working memory health models, the depicted covariates were consistently significant across all models.
Note that the income-to-needs ratio is only included in the scarcity models.
For sex, we coded females as 1 and males as 0.

This study tracked individuals and their environments over approximately a decade, combining self-reported measures from the LISS panel with administrative records from CBS registers to examine associations between adversity and cognition.

Across both the executive functioning and working memory samples, we find that self-report and registry-based adversity measures are only moderately correlated, replicating patterns documented in the broader literature 13, 22, 36, [49] [50] [51] [52] .
text.formatted: Across both the executive functioning and working memory samples, we find that self-report and registry-based adversity measures are only moderately correlated, replicating patterns documented in the broader literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[49]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[50]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[51]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[52]</ref> .

text.text: Critically, although associations with administrative and selfreport measures converged for some cognitive outcomes, they diverged for others.
Patterns of convergence and divergence differed across cognitive outcomes.
For working memory capacity, self-reported and administrative neighborhood threat showed opposite associations (a same-construct, data-source-dependent reversal).

For executive functioning, the divergence occurred across adversity dimensions: administrative unpredictability was positively associated with information processing, while self-reported neighborhood threat was negatively associated.
These two patterns are related but distinct, and we discuss them accordingly below.

Additionally, many of the associations between adversity measures (both self-report and administrative) and executive functioning parameters fell within the region of practical equivalence (intact cognitive performance).
Below we discuss what these convergent and divergent patterns reveal about how adversity is measured, experienced, and linked to cognition.
At the heart of our study is the comparison of self-report (LISS) and administrative (CBS) data.
Across both samples, self-report measures tend to correlate more strongly with other self-report measures than with administrative measures, and vice versa.
This suggests that the two data sources form partially distinct measurement clusters.

These findings are consistent with prior work documenting poor agreement between self-reported and administrative measures of adversity, and with the conclusion that they identify partially distinct groups at risk for worse outcomes 15 .
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with prior work documenting poor agreement between self-reported and administrative measures of adversity, and with the conclusion that they identify partially distinct groups at risk for worse outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> .

text.text: Further linking our adversity measures to cognition, we find stronger associations (as indexed by the absolute standardized effect) with self-reported adversity measures compared to administrative measures, irrespective of cognitive outcome.

Thus, our results deviate from prior work reporting that perceptions of adversity were more strongly related to attention shifting, whereas objective measures were more strongly related to working memory 61 .
text.formatted: Thus, our results deviate from prior work reporting that perceptions of adversity were more strongly related to attention shifting, whereas objective measures were more strongly related to working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">61</ref> .

text.text: One important difference between this work and our study is that the objective measures were derived from structured interviews (e.g. tabulating the number of moves), thereby still being self-reported.
Although smaller in magnitude, we also observe significant associations between cognitive outcomes and administrative records.
However, the direction of these associations is sometimes opposite of those observed for self-report measures.

Specifically, we find that self-reported neighborhood threat and the self-report adversity composite are negatively associated with both working memory capacity and general information processing, potentially in line with a deficit pattern.
Further aligning with these patterns, we observe a negative association between administrative crime victimization and information processing.

In contrast, administrative neighborhood threat is positively associated with working memory capacity, and administrative unpredictability in crime rates is positively associated with information processing, potentially consistent with performance enhancements.

Importantly, the positive association with unpredictability and the negative association with self-reported neighborhood threat reflect divergence between different adversity dimensions for information processing, not a same-construct reversal across data sources as for working memory capacity.

Together, these findings suggest that the relationship between adversity and cognition is complex: the data source, adversity dimension, and cognitive outcome can all moderate the direction and magnitude of associations.

However, we note that our significant associations with administrative adversity measures show small effect sizes that only just fall outside the practical equivalence band of ±0.10, highlighting the need for replication.

At the same time, we find that many adversity associations fall within the region of practical equivalence, particularly for CBS-derived administrative neighborhood threat and LISS selfreported health issues in the executive functioning sample.
One possibility is that adversity does not affect brain function and structure in a way that impacts these cognitive abilities, even though it may alter underlying processes [53] [54] [55] .
text.formatted: One possibility is that adversity does not affect brain function and structure in a way that impacts these cognitive abilities, even though it may alter underlying processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[53]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[54]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[55]</ref> .

text.text: Alternatively, intact performance might reflect a combination of impairment and adaptive processes, where impairment processes generally lower cognition, while adaptive processes boost certain relevant abilities (the net effect being intact performance), but not other abilities (thus, lower performance) 57 .
text.formatted: Alternatively, intact performance might reflect a combination of impairment and adaptive processes, where impairment processes generally lower cognition, while adaptive processes boost certain relevant abilities (the net effect being intact performance), but not other abilities (thus, lower performance) <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">57</ref> .

text.text: Either way, intact performance is inconsistent with a deficit perspective alone, which predicts negative associations with adversity.
Our application of unpredictability statistics to longitudinal administrative crime data is a novel contribution.
The predominantly positive associations among unpredictability indices are consistent with prior work applying this framework to other data sources, supporting the validity of the approach 44 .
text.formatted: The predominantly positive associations among unpredictability indices are consistent with prior work applying this framework to other data sources, supporting the validity of the approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">44</ref> .

text.text: The exception (not computed in that prior work)-entropy's consistent negative associations with other indices-implies that our residential crime time series are likely either characterized by infrequent, abrupt spikes combined with low variability, or by high, sustained, chronic variability.
In a sensitivity analysis (see methods), the significant positive association between unpredictability and information processing remained even after removing entropy from the construct.

From this we infer that the association is not driven by entropy and that, in our sample, chronic variability in crime rates experienced at the neighborhood level may weigh more heavily than episodic, abrupt disruptions.
This positive association between unpredictability and general information processing is predicted neither by adaptation frameworks nor by deficit frameworks, and warrants replication 66 .
text.formatted: This positive association between unpredictability and general information processing is predicted neither by adaptation frameworks nor by deficit frameworks, and warrants replication <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">66</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, this effect was sensitive to preprocessing decisions, particularly the imputation of zeros, which artificially stabilized some time series and reversed the association.

This sensitivity underscores the importance of transparent reporting of preprocessing choices in unpredictability research, and points to the need for further methodological work on how to handle missing data in time series data.
We further observe consistent indirect associations among covariates and cognitive outcomes across models, which replicate well-established findings.
Age-related decline in working memory capacity and the positive association between education and information processing are well-supported in previous research [67] [68] [69] .
text.formatted: Age-related decline in working memory capacity and the positive association between education and information processing are well-supported in previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[67]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[68]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">[69]</ref> .

text.text: The positive association between income-toneeds ratio and working memory updating is consistent with a large literature linking socioeconomic status to executive functioning [70] [71] [72] .
text.formatted: The positive association between income-toneeds ratio and working memory updating is consistent with a large literature linking socioeconomic status to executive functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">[70]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">[71]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">[72]</ref> .

text.text: More surprising are the consistent negative associations between education and working memory updating across models.
This pattern warrants cautious interpretation given the correlational nature of these associations.
It is possible that unmeasured confounders, or confounders we could not measure precisely enough, are responsible for this negative association rather than a true underlying relationship.

Comparing individual-and neighborhood-level adversity measures, we find that associations with cognitive outcomes mainly occur for neighborhood-level measures, or for those which include neighborhood-level indicators (administrative neighborhood threat, administrative unpredictability in neighborhood threat, self-reported neighborhood threat, self-reported adversity composite).
These findings replicate previous work in these samples 8, 45 .
text.formatted: These findings replicate previous work in these samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">45</ref> .

text.text: However, as noted above, while self-reported neighborhood adversity measures tend to be negatively associated with cognitive outcomes, the opposite is true for administrative measures (except for crime victimization).

These results contrast with a growing body of research linking objective neighborhood deprivation indices to lower working memory and executive function performance in adulthood, with effects persisting after adjustment for individual-level socioeconomic status 73 .
text.formatted: These results contrast with a growing body of research linking objective neighborhood deprivation indices to lower working memory and executive function performance in adulthood, with effects persisting after adjustment for individual-level socioeconomic status <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">73</ref> .

text.text: Our findings add nuance to this picture.
It is not simply that objective neighborhood adversity impairs cognition; rather, the nature of the adversity measure matters.

Individual crime victimization-a more direct and proximal form of adversity that may or may not occur at the neighborhood level-was associated with less efficient information processing (a performance deficit), whereas exposure to higher average crime rates across residential histories was associated with better working memory capacity (a performance enhancement).

This result may be consistent with an adaptationist perspective: sustained exposure to threatening environments may adaptively tailor cognitive abilities to environmental demands, while direct victimization may carry costs that outweigh any such functional benefits.
However, we emphasize that this adaptationist account is one of several post-hoc explanations for a pattern not predicted a priori by either the deficit or adaptation frameworks.

An equally parsimonious account is residential selection: cognitively or economically advantaged individuals may differentially select into, or be better able to leave, higher-crime neighborhoods for reasons not fully captured by education and income-toneeds.

Our cross-sectional outcome assessment precludes distinguishing environmental effects from selection effects, and we treat the adaptationist interpretation as hypothesisgenerating rather than supported.

Zooming out, our main result, the observed divergence between associations with self-reports and administrative records, suggests that both sources may index meaningfully different aspects of adversity exposure.
Self-reports often capture individuals' perceptions of their environment, which are shaped by appraisal and affective response.
Administrative records, by contrast, capture the objective exposure to adversity, irrespective of how that exposure is experienced.
These insights dovetail with contemporary discussions about the importance of distinguishing between objectively experienced and subjectively perceived adversity 11, 74 .
text.formatted: These insights dovetail with contemporary discussions about the importance of distinguishing between objectively experienced and subjectively perceived adversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">74</ref> .

text.text: We acknowledge that the broader thesis, that objective experiences and subjective perceptions can have different outcomes, is well-established in health and developmental psychopathology 15, 22, 36 .
text.formatted: We acknowledge that the broader thesis, that objective experiences and subjective perceptions can have different outcomes, is well-established in health and developmental psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">36</ref> .

text.text: Our contribution is to extend this question to adult cognition, where the literature contrasting self-report and administrative measures is sparse.

The sameconstruct reversal we observe for working memory capacity is, to our knowledge, novel in this domain, though the effect size is modest and replication is needed before strong conclusions can be drawn.
But how does the same neighborhood put individuals on different trajectories of meaning-making and perceptions of neighborhood threat?
One contributing factor is individuals' mental health, which can color their perceptions and interpretation of adverse experiences.

Previous work found, for example, that mental health was more strongly predicted by subjective neighborhood perceptions, whereas physical and social health outcomes were more strongly predicted by objective neighborhood features 75 .
text.formatted: Previous work found, for example, that mental health was more strongly predicted by subjective neighborhood perceptions, whereas physical and social health outcomes were more strongly predicted by objective neighborhood features <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">75</ref> .

text.text: Although our study did not include mental health, it is possible that individuals' mental health mediated the negative association between self-reported neighborhood threat and cognitive outcomes reported here.

To test this possibility, future work could extend the present study by incorporating mental health and other physical outcome measures to better understand the diverging effects between self-report and administrative adversity measures.
Our study contributes to an ongoing debate about how adversity should be operationalized.
On the one hand, cumulative risk approaches advocate for 'lumping' diverse adversities into a single index.

On the other hand, dimensional models 'split' adversity into dimensions, such as deprivation, threat, and unpredictability which may have distinct associations with neural and cognitive development 11, 76, 77 .
text.formatted: On the other hand, dimensional models 'split' adversity into dimensions, such as deprivation, threat, and unpredictability which may have distinct associations with neural and cognitive development <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">76,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">77</ref> .

text.text: Our results can inform both of these approaches.
The selfreport adversity composite (a singular index) shows a negative association with cognition, suggesting that cumulative perceived adversity carries cognitive costs.
Notably, only one of the individual self-report adversity measures showed a significant negative association with the same outcome.
Examining the CBS composite measure, we find no association between cumulative administrative adversity and cognition.

Yet, our individual measures did reveal significant associations, and moreover, not all adversity measures pointed in the same direction: administrative neighborhood threat was associated with enhanced working memory performance and the administrative crime victimization with lowered performance.
Lumping these together would not only obscure this divergence, but in our case even entirely hide the association between administrative adversity measures and cognition.
Recent work 11, 74, 78 argues that both lumping and splitting have limitations, calling for frameworks that attend to how adversity is experienced and interpreted by the individual.
text.formatted: Recent work <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">74,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">78</ref> argues that both lumping and splitting have limitations, calling for frameworks that attend to how adversity is experienced and interpreted by the individual.

text.text: We have taken initial steps towards such a framework by combining longitudinal administrative data with self-reported perceptions within the same individuals.

Our finding that objective exposure and subjective perception of the same adversity dimension (neighborhood threat) are associated with cognitive outcomes in opposite directions may be the clearest illustration of why this distinction matters.

The same neighborhood, objectively characterized by high crime rates, might be experienced as threatening and cognitively taxing by one individual, while another-perhaps someone who has developmentally adapted to that environment across years of residence-may show no such cognitive costs, or even strengths.
Our study has five main limitations.
The first concerns scope, specifically generalizability across contexts and ages.
We have studied a generalizable Dutch sample.
However, it is an open question to what extent our findings generalize to other cultures and countries, including those that do not include universal schooling (e.g. from rural communities) 79 .
text.formatted: However, it is an open question to what extent our findings generalize to other cultures and countries, including those that do not include universal schooling (e.g. from rural communities) <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">79</ref> .

text.text: Additionally, as our measurement period excludes childhood, there is a question about the generalizability across development.
Previous work has shown that the associations between adversity and cognition may differ in magnitude and direction depending on the developmental period during which adversity is experienced 31 .
text.formatted: Previous work has shown that the associations between adversity and cognition may differ in magnitude and direction depending on the developmental period during which adversity is experienced <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">31</ref> .

text.text: Second, administrative data are not perfectly objective.
They can be influenced by various types of selection and reporting biases at the geographical level (e.g. which acts get reported) and the individual level (e.g. who gets investigated) 80, 81 .
text.formatted: They can be influenced by various types of selection and reporting biases at the geographical level (e.g. which acts get reported) and the individual level (e.g. who gets investigated) <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">80,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">81</ref> .

text.text: Third, while our use of residential histories to derive neighborhood-level crime indicators is a methodological advance, actual exposure to neighborhood crime is not fully captured by residential location alone: mobility within neighborhoods, time spent outside the home, and social networks all shape effective exposure.
Fourth, the moderate correlations between LISS and CBS measures, while consistent with prior literature, also mean that neither source fully captures the respective adversity dimension.
Fifth, our crosssectional outcome assessment precludes causal inference.

In particular, the associations we find are compatible both with selection effects (individuals with higher cognitive ability selecting into different neighborhoods) and with environmental effects (experienced conditions influencing cognitive performance).
Longitudinal designs with repeated cognitive assessments, or quasi-experimental designs exploiting exogenous variation in neighborhood assignment (e.g.
Moving to Opportunity study 35 ), are needed to disentangle selection from environmental effects.
text.formatted: Moving to Opportunity study <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">35</ref> ), are needed to disentangle selection from environmental effects.

text.text: We therefore caution against interpreting the positive administrative associations as evidence of cognitive enhancement caused by adversity exposure.
Our findings highlight four crucial directions for future research.

First, the divergent patterns across data sources call for studies that explicitly model the gap between objective exposure and subjective perception as a variable of interest in its own right: individuals who perceive their environment as more threatening than objective indicators may be particularly at risk for worse outcomes.

Second, life-course modeling approaches that use the full temporal structure of administrative records could reveal whether the timing of adversity exposure, not just its cumulative level, moderates cognitive outcomes, thus providing insights into sensitive periods for adversity exposure 82, 83 .
text.formatted: Second, life-course modeling approaches that use the full temporal structure of administrative records could reveal whether the timing of adversity exposure, not just its cumulative level, moderates cognitive outcomes, thus providing insights into sensitive periods for adversity exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">82,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">83</ref> .

text.text: Third, extending our present study to include childhood measures would allow us to explore whether adversity-cognition associations reflect developmental adaptation or adult-stage processes.

Finally, the unpredictability framework 38 applied to neighborhood crime could be extended to other administrative time series (e.g. income, health issues) to build a richer, multi-domain picture of environmental unpredictability across the lifespan.
text.formatted: Finally, the unpredictability framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">38</ref> applied to neighborhood crime could be extended to other administrative time series (e.g. income, health issues) to build a richer, multi-domain picture of environmental unpredictability across the lifespan.

text.text: In conclusion, our study shows that self-report and administrative adversity measures capture distinct facets of individuals' lived experiences, and that these facets are associated with cognitive outcomes in different, sometimes opposing, directions.

Perceived adversity is associated with lower cognitive performance, and objective exposure to neighborhood crime is sometimes associated with performance enhancements, particularly in working memory capacity.
These findings underscore the value of combining subjective and objective measures within the same individuals across time.

Our results echo recent calls for theoretical frameworks that can accommodate the possibility that the same environmental conditions carry different cognitive consequences depending on how they are experienced 11, 74, 78.
text.formatted: Our results echo recent calls for theoretical frameworks that can accommodate the possibility that the same environmental conditions carry different cognitive consequences depending on how they are experienced <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">74,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">78</ref>.
